style_2_guidelines.guideline_authority: IDSA Practice Guidelines & WHO Antimicrobial Management Protocols (2024)

clinical_targets.goal: Documented pathogen clearance / negative repeat cultures
Afebrile for ≥ 48 hours, normalization of leukocytosis and vital signs
De-escalation to targeted narrow-spectrum oral therapy as soon as clinically stable

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Long COVID focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Long COVID require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Long COVID.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.
Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.
Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.
Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Dose-adjust beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, and aminoglycosides according to estimated creatinine clearance (CrCl).
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Monitor liver enzymes with macrolides, azoles, rifamycins, and isoniazid.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Penicillins, cephalosporins, and azithromycin are preferred; avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines.
special_populations.elderly: High risk of Clostridioides difficile colitis; avoid prolonged broad-spectrum empiric courses.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is long COVID? COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) is an illness caused by a virus. Many people get better within a few days or weeks after being infected with the virus. But if you have symptoms that last for at least three months or more, you may have long COVID. Long COVID is a chronic (long-lasting) condition. It includes a wide range of symptoms or conditions that can range from mild to severe. You may: Have symptoms that linger for weeks, months, or even years Seem to recover from COVID-19 but then see your symptoms return Develop new symptoms or new health conditions within a few months of having COVID-19 There are several other names for long COVID. It can also be called post-COVID conditions, long-haul COVID, and post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 (PASC). Who is more likely to develop long COVID? Anyone who had COVID-19, whether it was severe or mild, can have long-lasting symptoms. But you are at higher risk of long COVID if you: Are female. Are Hispanic or Latino. Had severe COVID-19 illness, especially if you were hospitalized or needed intensive care. Had other health conditions before you got COVID-19. Did not get a COVID-19 vaccine . Had multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS) during or after COVID-19. MIS is a rare but serious condition in which different parts of your body become inflamed. What are the symptoms of long COVID? Long COVID does not affect everyone the same way. It can cause various types and combinations of symptoms in different people. The symptoms may affect different parts of the body, for example, you could have: General symptoms, such as fatigue and fever Respiratory symptoms, such as trouble breathing and cough Heart symptoms, such as chest pain and palpitations Neurologic symptoms such as trouble thinking and concentrating ("brain fog"), headaches , and sleep problems Digestive symptoms such as diarrhea , constipation , and stomach pain Some people may have a wide variety of symptoms that are similar to those of other conditions, such as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Most people's symptoms slowly improve over time. But for some people, the symptoms can last weeks, months, or longer. Sometimes the symptoms are severe enough to result in disability , including in children. When long COVID affects multiple organs in your body, you may be at higher risk of developing other conditions. These include diabetes , heart diseases , and neurologic conditions . How is long COVID diagnosed? There is no specific test for long COVID. To find out if you have long COVID, your health care provider: Will ask about your medical history. This includes asking if you have had a diagnosis of COVID-19, either based on a positive test, symptoms, or exposure. Will do a physical exam. May order blood and imaging tests. Some of the symptoms of long COVID may be hard to explain. The results of blood and imaging tests may be normal. And people who have unexplained symptoms may sometimes be misunderstood by their providers. So, it can take some time to get a diagnosis. What are the treatments for long COVID? There is no specific treatment for long COVID. You and your provider can work together to create a personal care plan to help manage your symptoms and improve your quality of life. Can long COVID be prevented? The best way to prevent long COVID is to avoid getting COVID-19. Staying up to date with vaccines (including boosters) against COVID-19 can help prevent COVID-19 infection and protect against severe illness. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
style_3_monograph.treatment: There is no specific cure for long COVID. Treatment will depend on your symptoms and may include: A progressive exercise program Physical therapy Occupational therapy Speech and language therapy Neurological rehabilitation (for cognitive symptoms) Pulmonary rehabilitation Mental health care Medicines to help manage symptoms You may want to consider joining a clinical trial for long COVID. A clinical trial is a study using people who agree to participate in new tests or treatments. Clinical trials help researchers know whether a new treatment works well and is safe. The National Institutes of Health has created RECOVER: Researching COVID to Enhance Recovery where you can learn more about long COVID clinical trials near you. For the most up-to-date information on long COVID, visit these websites: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: Long COVID basics -- www.cdc.gov/covid/long-term-effects/ Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: CDC science and the public health approach to long COVID -- www.cdc.gov/covid/php/long-covid/
